b: An autoimmune disease : TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies (TRAb) stimulate the gland to make hormone and grow (a diffuse goitre). Female to male ratio 5:1 to 10:1 , peak age 20 to 50, strong hereditary component (HLA-DR3, other autoimmune
The diagnosis is mainly clinical (symptoms and signs), confirmed by tests.

General: weight loss despite an increased appetite, heat intolerance and excessive sweating, fatigue, and a warm moist skin; palms warm, moist and hyperaemic; Plummer's nails (onycholysis) ; alopecia and vitiligo.
CVS: palpitations, sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation , a collapsing pulse, isolated systolic hypertension , and congestive cardiac failure (high-output) in the elderly.
GIT: hyperdefecation (increased frequency of stools), and diarrhoea. Respiratory: may exacerbate asthma; dyspnoea.

qs.q: An adolescent is diagnosed with Graves disease. Which HLA allele carries a 7-fold relative risk for this condition?
o: HLA-DR3 allele carrying a 7-fold relative risk
HLA-DQ2 allele conferring pediatric susceptibility
HLA-A2 allele linked to endocrine disorders
HLA-B27 allele carrying significant autoimmune risk
qs.e: Graves disease is strongly associated with HLA-B8 and HLA-DR3, with the latter carrying a 7-fold relative risk. HLA-B27 is linked to other conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis rather than Graves disease.

qs.q: What is the main pathological mechanism by which TRSAbs cause unregulated thyroid hormone synthesis in Graves disease?
o: They bind to and activate G protein-coupled TSH receptors, increasing cyclic AMP production.
They inhibit the negative feedback of thyroid hormones on the anterior pituitary gland.
They block the degradation of thyroxine-binding globulin in the peripheral circulation.
They directly destroy thyroid follicular cells, causing a massive release of stored colloid.
qs.e: TRSAbs bind to and stimulate the TSH receptor, resulting in increased cyclic AMP production and subsequent thyroid hyperplasia. The other options do not describe the direct mechanism of these specific stimulating antibodies.

qs.q: A pediatric patient with thyrotoxicosis undergoes laboratory evaluation. Which antibody assays are 96-97% sensitive and 99% specific for diagnosing Graves disease?
o: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin and Thyrotropin-binding inhibitory immunoglobulin
Thyroid hormone receptor-beta blocking antibodies and stimulating immunoglobulins
Microsomal antibodies and retro-orbital fibroblast inhibitory antibodies
Anti-thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
qs.e: TSI and TBII assays measure receptor-stimulating activity and binding capacity, respectively, and are highly sensitive and specific for Graves disease. Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin are classically associated with autoimmune thyroiditis rather than primary diagnostic confirmation of Graves.

qs.q: Which of the following ocular manifestations is true regarding children with Graves disease?
o: Children experience significantly more severe retro-orbital pain and vision loss than adults.
Eye findings are completely absent in pediatric Graves disease because receptors are absent.
Eye findings occur in the majority of children, but symptoms are much milder than in adults.
Ophthalmopathy never occurs in pediatric patients and is strictly restricted to adults over 40.
qs.e: While 50-75% of children with Graves disease have eye findings, their symptoms are much milder than those seen in adults. TSH receptors are indeed present in retro-orbital adipocytes of children.

qs.q: A newborn delivered by a mother with a history of Graves disease presents with tachycardia, irritability, and poor weight gain. What is the expected natural history of this infant's condition?
o: It worsens steadily over childhood as endogenous antibodies rise.
It is transitory and resolves as maternal antibodies are cleared.
It remains asymptomatic initially and presents during adolescence.
It persists lifelong and requires definitive surgical thyroidectomy.
qs.e: Neonatal hyperthyroidism caused by transplacental maternal antibodies is transitory and clears as the maternal antibodies degrade over several weeks. It does not reflect a permanent primary defect in the infant's own thyroid gland.

qs.q: Toxic multinodular goiter differs from Graves' disease by which of the following features?
o: It occurs in older patients with long-standing goiter and lacks TSI antibodies
It is significantly more common in young women aged 20 to 30 years
It is directly driven by circulating thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins
It frequently presents clinically with classic infiltrative ophthalmopathy
qs.e: Toxic multinodular goiter results from autonomous function of multiple nodules in a pre-existing goiter without TSI antibodies or eye signs. It typically presents in older adults living in iodine-deficient regions.

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman undergoes a thyroidectomy for Graves disease. Histologic examination of the thyroid gland shows follicular epithelial cells that are tall and columnar instead of the normal cuboidal shape. This finding is best explained by which of the following processes?
o: Hyperplasia with hypertrophy
Neoplastic transformation process
Metaplasia of the epithelium
Anaplasia of the follicular cells
Dysplasia of the thyroid cells
qs.e: In Graves disease, excessive TSH receptor stimulation leads to both increased number (hyperplasia) and increased size (hypertrophy) of follicular cells, causing them to become tall and columnar. This is a physiologic adaptation to hormonal stimulation, not a neoplastic or metaplastic change.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of Graves' disease?
o: Toxic nodular goitre
Exophthalmos
Diffuse goitre
Antibodies to TSH receptor
qs.e: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder causing diffuse toxic goitre and hyperthyroidism, typically mediated by TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb). Exophthalmos is a characteristic feature. Toxic nodular goitre (Plummer's disease) is a different cause of hyperthyroidism.

es.q: Discuss the immunopathogenesis of Graves disease in children.
es.m:
**Immunopathogenesis**
- TRSAbs bind and activate TSHR, stimulating cAMP production.
- cAMP drives thyroid hyperplasia and unregulated hormone synthesis.
- B‑cell activation leads to plasma cells producing TRSAbs.
- CD4+ T helper cells predominate in dense lymphoid aggregates; CD8+ cytotoxic cells in lower density areas.
- Failure of T‑suppressor cells allows sensitized T helper cells to interact with B cells.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by TSH‑receptor antibodies, producing diffuse goitre, eye signs and systemic hypermetabolism. Diagnosis hinges on suppressed TSH, high free T4/T3 and positive TSI. Management balances antithyroid drugs, definitive therapy and eye care.

sections.p: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroidism where TSH‑receptor stimulating antibodies (TSI) activate the thyroid, causing diffuse goitre and systemic hypermetabolism. Diagnosis requires suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, and a positive TSI or TRAb test. Clinical features such as exophthalmos or pretibial myxoedema strongly support the diagnosis.
b: TSH <0.1 mIU/L with high free T4/T3

sections.p: Severity is staged by clinical impact: mild (stable symptoms), moderate (symptom‑driven treatment), severe (thyroid storm or ophthalmopathy). Ophthalmopathy is graded by the NOSPECS system, guiding eye‑specific therapy.
b: Mild: stable, moderate: symptomatic, severe: thyroid storm or eye disease

sections.p: The primary cause is autoimmune activation of TSH receptors by TSI. Other triggers include iodine excess, pregnancy, stress, and certain drugs (amiodarone, interferon). In low‑resource settings, infections such as HIV or TB may precipitate or mimic disease.

Patients present with weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, and a diffuse, non‑tender goitre. Eye signs—exophthalmos, lid lag, diplopia—are classic. Pretibial myxoedema is a rare but specific sign.

Key investigations confirm hyperthyroidism, exclude other causes, and assess eye disease. In resource‑limited settings, a simple TSH and free T4/T3 may suffice; if unavailable, a clinical diagnosis can guide empiric therapy.

Urgent red flags include atrial fibrillation, heart failure, thyroid storm, or severe ophthalmopathy. Complications can be cardiovascular, ophthalmic, or neuropsychiatric. Early recognition prevents mortality.

Treat the underlying autoimmune drive with antithyroid drugs (methimazole preferred; PTU if pregnancy). Monitor for agranulocytosis. Definitive therapy—radioactive iodine or surgery—is reserved for refractory or severe cases. Eye disease is managed with steroids and orbital decompression if needed.

t.b: Used in pregnancy or severe disease
For large goitre or suspicion of cancer

sections.p: Patients need regular TSH and free T4 monitoring until euthyroid. Eye disease requires ophthalmology follow‑up. Prevention focuses on avoiding iodine excess and managing autoimmune triggers.
Other causes of hyperthyroidism—tissue‑damage (thyroiditis), iodine excess, factitious thyrotoxicosis—lack the characteristic eye signs and TSI positivity.
TSH may be normal in early disease or in the presence of thyroid hormone resistance. Free T4 can be falsely low if protein binding is altered. Eye signs may be subtle in early disease.
Seek urgent care if symptoms of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, or thyroid storm develop, or if eye disease threatens vision.

faq.a: Antithyroid drugs can induce remission, but definitive cure requires radioactive iodine or surgery.

faq.q: Why is exophthalmos seen in Graves but not other hyperthyroidism?
faq.a: Autoimmune inflammation of orbital tissues driven by TSH‑receptor antibodies causes eye swelling.

faq.q: Is pregnancy safe with Graves disease?
faq.a: Yes, but antithyroid drugs must be chosen carefully; methimazole is preferred, PTU used if severe or early pregnancy.
